benchmark_type_evidence: we introduce the Cross-lingual TRansfer Evaluation of Multilingual Encoders (XTREME) benchmark, a multi-task benchmark for evaluating the cross-lingual generalization capabilities of multilingual representations across 40 languages and 9 tasks
brief_description: XTREME (Cross-lingual TRansfer Evaluation of Multilingual Encoders) is a multi-task benchmark for evaluating the cross-lingual generalization capabilities of multilingual representations. It covers 40 typologically diverse languages spanning 12 language families and includes 9 tasks across classification, structured prediction, question answering, and sentence retrieval.

datasets.annotation_method: Crowd-sourced English data (MultiNLI) translated to 10 other languages by professional translators

datasets.notes: Test sets are translations of English data. Training uses MultiNLI English data.

data_creator_info.evidence: A subset of the PAWS dev and test sets (Zhang et al., 2019) was translated to six other languages by professional translators and is used for evaluation, while the PAWS training set is used for training.

datasets.notes: Test sets are translations of English data.

data_creator_info.evidence: We use POS tagging data from the Universal Dependencies v2.5 (Nivre et al., 2018) treebanks, which cover 90 languages. Each word is assigned one of 17 universal POS tags.

datasets.annotation_method: Automatic annotation using knowledge base properties, cross-lingual and anchor links, self-training, and data selection

data_creator_info.evidence: Named entities in Wikipedia were automatically annotated with LOC, PER, and ORG tags in IOB2 format using a combination of knowledge base properties, cross-lingual and anchor links, self-training, and data selection.

datasets.annotation_method: Subset of English SQuAD v1.1 dev set translated into 10 other languages by professional translators

datasets.notes: Test sets are translations of English SQuAD data. Training uses SQuAD v1.1 English data.

datasets.translation_method: Automatically mined parallel sentences from Wikipedia; crowdsourced annotations in English; questions translated and answer spans aligned in target languages
datasets.annotation_method: Automatic mining of parallel sentences + crowdsourced English annotations + translation and alignment of questions/answers

data_creator_info.evidence: The evaluation data for English and six other languages was obtained by automatically mining target language sentences that are parallel to sentences in English from Wikipedia, crowd-sourcing annotations in English, and translating the question and aligning the answer spans in the target languages.

datasets.notes: Context passages are native (mined from Wikipedia in target languages). Questions are crowdsourced in English and translated/aligned. Training uses SQuAD v1.1 English data.

datasets.variant_notes: Simplified version using only gold passage as context, excluding unanswerable questions
datasets.annotation_method: Questions written by native speakers without seeing the answers; independently annotated

data_creator_info.creator_affiliation: INSUFFICIENT_INFO: Paper references Clark et al. 2020 but does not detail annotator affiliations
data_creator_info.evidence: questions have been written without seeing the answers, leading to 3x and 2x less lexical overlap compared to XQuAD and MLQA respectively

datasets.notes: More challenging than XQuAD and MLQA due to questions written without seeing answers. Gold passage version simplifies the primary TyDi QA task.

datasets.annotation_method: Parallel sentence extraction from comparable corpora between English and four other languages

data_creator_info.evidence: The goal of the second and third shared task of the workshop on Building and Using Parallel Corpora is to extract parallel sentences from a comparable corpus between English and four other languages.

datasets.notes: Evaluated without fine-tuning using cosine similarity. Train and test splits provided for each language pair.

datasets.variant_notes: Paper claims 33-language intersection with XTREME's 40 languages, but results tables show evaluation on 36 non-English target languages

data_creator_info.evidence: We use the Tatoeba dataset (Artetxe & Schwenk, 2019), which consists of up to 1,000 English-aligned sentence pairs covering 122 languages.

datasets.notes: 122 languages in full dataset. Nearest neighbour retrieval using cosine similarity. Error rate is the evaluation metric.

all_annotators_native_speakers.evidence: Only TyDiQA-GoldP clearly uses native speaker annotators. WikiANN is fully automatic. XNLI, PAWS-X, XQuAD use professional translators. MLQA uses English crowdworkers.

annotator_workforce.evidence: Paper aggregates existing datasets and does not create new annotations. Annotator details are in original dataset papers.

cultural_flags.english_centricity_notes: XTREME is explicitly English-centric: 'XTREME focuses on the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer scenario, where annotated training data is provided in English but none is provided in the language to which systems must transfer.' Three of nine datasets (XNLI, PAWS-X, XQuAD) are direct translations from English. MLQA questions originate in English. All models are trained on English data.

notably_excluded: Most of Sub-Saharan Africa (only Swahili and Yoruba)
geographic_representation.evidence: 40 languages from 12 families and two isolates. Indo-European languages heavily overrepresented (~17 of 40).
